newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL overnight ends down at 10/15 pct.
newsitem.headline: KL overnight ends down at 10/15 pct.

text.p: The overnight interbank rate eased to 10/15 percent in late trading as demand ebbed due to the maturity of a 500 million ringgit Bank Negara bill issue, dealers said on Thursday.
They said the overnight eased from a high of 15/20 percent in early afternoon as banks in a hurry to cover their positions bid at the previous levels.
"The fall in other interbank rates earlier also weakened sentiment," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.
All interbank rates could fall further on Friday due to the maturity of another 500 million ringgit in Bank Negara bills.
Earlier, other interbank rates declined after the bill maturity.
One-week and two-week interbank rates were down at 9.0/10.0 percent against 10/15 percent on Tuesday.
One-month money was down at 8.0/8.5 percent against 9.0/9.5 percent on Tuesday, three-month declined to 7.5/8.0 percent against 8.0/8.5 percent and six-month was at 7.5/8.0 percent against 8.5/9.0.
The market was closed on Wednesday for a Buddhist festival.
Thursday's maturity of Bank Negara bills has already been rolled over through an issue on Tuesday.
"Many people think that the rates are not sustainable at the high levels they have reached in the last few days," said a dealer with a large Malaysian bank.
"That is why there are a lot of lenders in the market, which has pulled down the rates," he said.
But many dealers were uncertain about the near-term trend.
"I am not sure if rates will fall because the market is facing too big a shortage to be covered by the maturities," said a dealer with another Malaysian bank.
One dealer said it was possible the central bank was keeping rates high, partly as a move to fend off a fresh attack on the ringgit by speculators on Wednesday, a holiday in Malaysia.
At prevailing rates, it would be too expensive for players to maintain short ringgit positions, he said.

The rise in interbank rates started last Thursday after Bank Negara intervened aggressively in the foreign exchange market to stem the slide of the ringgit. The central bank was said to have sold around $1 billion worth of dollars.
The intervention drained liquidity from the system, causing the market to be short and interbank rates to rise to unusually high levels.
Interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange closed higher across the board on expectation of a further fall in interest rates, futures dealers said.
The three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) contract for June 1997 was up six at 92.54, or an implied yield of 7.46 percent.
September 1997 contract was up six at 92.58, or 7.42 percent and December was up six at 92.59, or 7.41 percent.
-- Madhav Reddy (603-230 7509) .
